contexts.display_text: A room is initially warmer than the outdoor air. Its heater is switched off and the room cools down.

duplicate-d689a7570b613016.hint: Connect the energy supplied during the chosen interval to the temperature rise over that same interval.
notes: With negligible losses, Pt = mcΔT, so a temperature–time slope is P/(mc). Use a representative straight-line section of the graph.
If heat loss is included, use net heating power. A plateau during a phase change uses latent heat, not mcΔT with a zero temperature rise.

duplicate-7b4589da961298a7.hint: Check the emitting area and use absolute temperature. The temperature dependence is much stronger than linear.
notes: Thermal emission power is P = εσAT⁴. For a sphere use 4πR²; for a black body ε = 1.
For ratios, keep any changes in emissivity and area as well as the fourth power of temperature. Net exchange with surroundings at Tₛ is εσA(T⁴ − Tₛ⁴) in the stated simple model.

duplicate-bd7d79dfba616c68.hint: Think about how energy passes between neighbouring particles, and whether mobile electrons are present.
notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.
For a steady uniform slab, transfer rate is kAΔT/L. Larger area or temperature difference increases the rate; greater thickness decreases it.

duplicate-b4d4593abf97ba97.hint: Compare the particle arrangement or energy-transfer rate, rather than assuming a sensation tells you the temperature.
notes: Temperature and rate of energy transfer are different. Metal can feel colder than plastic at the same temperature because it conducts energy away from skin faster.
Particle spacing and arrangement determine volume and density. Most solids are denser than their liquids, but water is a notable exception.

notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

duplicate-3b8fb93bf2092fd4.hint: Think about both the rate of wall collisions and the momentum change in each collision.
notes: Gas pressure is momentum transferred to the walls per unit time per unit area. Higher temperature increases typical molecular speeds and momentum transfer.
A smaller volume also increases collision frequency with the walls. Collisions between molecules alone are not the direct force exerted on a wall.

ibd-a88908df340c714d-q2:d.hint: Consider the system and its surroundings together. A local entropy decrease need not violate the second law.
notes: For reversible heat transfer at constant temperature, ΔS = Q_rev/T. A warming or cooling reservoir uses the sign of the heat it receives.
The total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease. Irreversible processes increase total entropy and reduce the energy available for useful work; energy itself is still conserved.
